You are an evidence extractor for an equity research desk. You read ONE news item and turn what it says into structured evidence cards. You only report what the text itself says. You do not use outside knowledge, you do not guess what happened later, and you do not forecast prices.

WATCHED COMPANIES (use exactly these tickers):
- NVDA: NVIDIA, Nvidia
- AAPL: Apple
- GOOGL: Alphabet, Google, GOOG
- META: Meta Platforms, Meta, Facebook
- AMZN: Amazon, AWS
- TSLA: Tesla
- MSTR: MicroStrategy, Strategy Inc
- COIN: Coinbase
- HOOD: Robinhood
- CRCL: Circle Internet, Circle

A text may name a company by its ticker, by its company name, or via a product ticker such as "2x Long NVDA ETF" (that counts as NVDA). Leveraged/inverse ETFs on a company count as that company. Companies not in the list above never get a name card.

CARD TYPES
- scope "name": the text says something specific about a watched company (its business, results, products, deals, guidance, analyst actions, regulation, management, or its own stock). One card per watched company, "tickers" = [that ticker]. A company that only appears in a list of movers or a passing mention with no information about it gets NO card.
- scope "sector": the text says something about an industry or theme but not about a specific watched company. "tickers" = [] and "sector" = one of: ai_semis, megacap_tech, crypto, fintech, ev_auto, other. At most 2 sector cards.
- scope "market": the text says something about the overall US stock market or risk appetite (Fed and rates, inflation data, geopolitics, index moves, broad flows). "tickers" = [] and "sector" = "". At most 1 market card.
If the text says nothing relevant to US equities, crypto or macro risk appetite, return {"cards": []}.

NO CARD for a watched company when it only appears:
- in a list of tickers, price changes, fund flows, positions or "representative stocks" where it gets a number or a few words and no reason specific to it;
- in advertisements, promotions, giveaways, disclaimers or navigation text;
- as a benchmark, comparison or background name in an article about another company.
Exception: if an article about another company states a concrete fact that directly affects the watched company (it signs a deal with it, becomes its customer or tenant, wins or loses business from it), give a name card with strength at most 0.4.

FIELDS (per card)
- stance: integer -2..2. The direction the reported information points for that company / sector / market. +2 clearly and strongly positive (e.g. large earnings beat with raised guidance, major contract, upgrade with a big target raise); +1 positive; 0 neutral, mixed or purely descriptive; -1 negative; -2 clearly and strongly negative. Judge the information, not the tone of the headline.
- strength: number 0..1. How material, specific and well-supported the information is for that subject. 0.1 = vague or passing; 0.4 = clear but modest; 0.7 = specific and material; 0.9 = major, confirmed, company-specific.
- horizon_h: integer hours the information is likely to stay relevant: 4-24 for intraday flow or sentiment; 24-72 for ordinary news; 72-240 for earnings, guidance, analyst actions, deals; up to 720 for structural changes.
- novelty: "new" if the text reports a development for the first time (an announcement, data release, deal, filing, analyst action, product news). "recap" if it summarises developments that are already known: weekly or daily roundups, previews of upcoming events, general outlook or opinion pieces. "post_hoc" if the text explains why a price ALREADY moved: titles or texts like "[Market Movement Analysis]", "[Market Movement Interpretation]", "X surges on <date>: ...", "why X stock fell today". Decide novelty per card: a card whose content is mainly that the stock or market already rose or fell (with or without reasons) is "post_hoc", even inside a daily roundup. A post_hoc card still gets the stance of the reasons it gives.
- summary: one English sentence, at most 200 characters, stating the information for that subject.
- quote: one contiguous verbatim excerpt (at most 25 words) copied from the text that supports the card. Copy it exactly: no paraphrase, no ellipses, no joining of separate sentences.

OUTPUT
Reply with one JSON object and nothing else:
{"cards": [{"scope": "name|sector|market", "tickers": ["NVDA"], "sector": "", "stance": 1, "strength": 0.6, "horizon_h": 72, "novelty": "new", "summary": "...", "quote": "..."}]}

TITLE: Crypto Rally, Bond Sell-Off: Where the Next Opportunities May Emerge

TEXT:
1.Asset Performance Last Week
Energy led the gains this week, providing the key backdrop for understanding moves across other asset classes. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rose 9.95% for the week to $91.70 and 21.02% over the month, while Brent crude gained 7.27% to $95.80 for the week and 20.72% over the month. The sharp rise in energy prices over the past two weeks has revived inflation expectations that had previously eased. This was the immediate catalyst for this week's global bond sell-off and is also one of the key variables shaping expectations for the September FOMC meeting.
Performance within crypto diverged, with Bitcoin regaining the lead. Bitcoin gained 2.50% for the week to $79,804 and 23.95% over the month, while Ethereum rose 0.62% for the week and 31.28% over the month. SOL declined 2.00% for the week, but remains up 39.17% over the month. At its current price, Bitcoin remains approximately 36.8% below its October 6, 2025 all-time high of $126,200. For clarity, weekly performance is measured from the August 28 close to the September 4 close, while monthly performance is measured from August 4 to September 4.
Precious metals edged higher, while the U.S. dollar weakened. Gold gained 0.97% for the week to $4521.50 and 10.40% over the month. It is worth noting that the current price is not an all-time high; its 2026 peak was $5586 on January 29. Silver rose 0.54% for the week and 12.15% over the month, while copper gained 1.79%. The U.S. Dollar Index fell 0.70% for the week to 99.00, while USD/KRW declined 1.80% and USD/JPY fell 0.25% to 158.92. The yen's appreciation reflected increased market pricing of a Bank of Japan rate hike, rather than developments on the U.S. dollar side.
────────────────────────────────────────
2. Global Bond Sell-Off
This week's sell-off was not confined to any single country's government bonds; it extended broadly across developed-market sovereign debts. On a weekly basis, the French 10-year yield rose 8.9 basis points, the U.S. 10-year yield increased 7.2 basis points, the German 10-year yield climbed 5.8 basis points, and the U.S. 30-year yield rose 4.0 basis points. The U.K. and Japanese 10-year yields declined 1.0 and 2.2 basis points, respectively, although both initially moved higher during the week before reversing. On a monthly basis, yields rose across all six maturities: France was up 30.8 basis points, Germany 22.1 basis points, the U.S. 10-year 17.0 basis points, the U.K. 15.8 basis points, the U.S. 30-year 7.2 basis points, and Japan 4.8 basis points.
Japan was at the epicenter of the sell-off. On September 2, the 10-year Japanese government bond (JGB) yield reached 3.0175%, crossing the 3% threshold for the first time since 1996. Over the past 12 months, the yield has risen 133.9 basis points, the largest increase among the six markets and well above the 74.6-basis-point rise in the U.S. 10-year yield over the same period. The significance lies less in the absolute level than in Japan's fiscal position: government debt exceeds 200% of GDP, while debt-servicing costs account for more than a quarter of government spending this fiscal year. Further increases in yields would therefore directly constrain Japan's fiscal space. Market pricing for a Bank of Japan rate hike on September 18 has risen to around 90%, while the yen strengthened past 156 against the U.S. dollar within two trading days.
Our view is that this sell-off is less about "how long will rates stay high?" and more about "what is sovereign credit worth?" The U.S. 10-year yield closed at 4.789% and the 30-year yield at 5.247%, both near the upper end of their ranges in the current cycle. As long as the underlying dynamics of fiscal deficits and long-term government bond supply remain unchanged, each disorderly rise in long-term yields could serve as a near-term catalyst for supply-constrained assets such as gold and Bitcoin. The other side of the equation, however, should not be overlooked: if short-term rates rise at the same time, valuations across long-duration assets, including crypto, will come under pressure. This creates an interim window in which crypto could face pressure alongside the broader rate shock before the longer-term support from sovereign credit concerns takes hold. The September 11 inflation data and September 15–16 policy meeting could mark the beginning of this window.
────────────────────────────────────────
3.Activity in Crypto Assets
The three strongest performers in crypto this week were all outside the major assets. On a weekly basis, PONS rose approximately 359%, ARB gained 50.97%, and UNI advanced 41.35%, compared with 2.50% for Bitcoin and 0.62% for Ethereum. On a monthly basis, PONS surged approximately 2915%, while ARB rose 64.44% and UNI gained 57.85%. Bitcoin and Ethereum were up 23.95% and 31.28%, respectively. PONS price data are based on the spot market, while data for the other four assets are sourced from Bitget's public market data API.
[...]
All three rallies can be traced to the same catalyst: the rapid expansion of a new blockchain ecosystem. Robinhood Chain, an Ethereum Layer 2 network launched in July 2026, is built on the Arbitrum Orbit technology stack. This has been a key driver behind ARB's roughly 90% rebound from its June all-time low. Uniswap has captured a large share of transaction routing on the network, with UNI now up more than 130% over the past 90 days. PONS, meanwhile, serves as a token issuance platform within the ecosystem. Daily new-token issuance approached 20,000 at the end of August, while early September saw a record $500 million in single-day trading volume and approximately $4 billion in cumulative volume. Its buyback-and-burn mechanism has now removed more than 28% of total supply.
[...]
4. Robinhood Chain On-Chain Data Analysis
[...]
Total value locked (TVL) has increased roughly 17-fold in two months. As of September 4, TVL on Robinhood Chain stood at $835.5 million, up 26.2% week over week and 107.3% month over month. On July 8, the figure was just $46.8 million. This is still a newly launched blockchain growing from a very low base, with no clear inflection point yet visible in the growth trajectory.
[...]
Robinhood Chain's trading volume has already surpassed that of two more established blockchains. In terms of seven-day decentralized exchange (DEX) volume, Robinhood Chain recorded $11.30 billion, up 105.7% week over week. BSC recorded $8.70 billion, up 19.9%, while Base posted $5.75 billion, down 19.6%, and Arbitrum $1.28 billion, down 16.9%. Just two months after launch, Robinhood Chain is already generating more trading volume than BSC, which has been operating for more than five years, and Base, which has been live for more than three years.
[...]
The gap in fees is even more pronounced than the gap in volume. Over the past seven days, protocols on Robinhood Chain generated $113.1 million in fees, equivalent to 4.7 times BSC's $24.14 million and 9.2 times Base's $12.25 million. On September 2, daily on-chain fees reached a record $4.45 million, a figure that also became a prominent topic on Korean-language social media this week.
[...]
Within crypto, PONS emerged as the asset with the broadest market consensus this week. It appeared across regional rankings and data sources in six countries and regions, compared with five appearances each for SOL and ARB. Among ARB's five appearances, a specific theme on Korean-language social media was "rising Robinhood Chain fees," consistent with the fee data discussed in Section 4. Taken together, the three high-consensus assets point to the same conclusion: crypto market attention this week was concentrated on a newly launched chain rather than on price moves in major assets.
